name: phantom-ai
description: Run the phantom CLI to sign in to Phantom AI, set up or start coding agents on it, add credit, cap what each key spends, and pick models. Use when the user asks for Phantom AI, phantom-1, or a payment or spending task in Phantom.
---

# Phantom AI

Phantom AI is an OpenAI-compatible API at `https://phantom.codes/v1`. The Phantom CLI (`phantom`) connects coding agents to it, keeps the user's keys, adds credit to their workspace and sets each key's caps and models. When you run it, its output goes through a pipe, so commands print JSON; add `--table` to get the screen a person sees. phantom refuses flags it doesn't know, so check `phantom <command> --help` for the names.

## Start an agent for one run

```bash
phantom login
phantom workspace status
phantom codex
phantom claude --key coding
phantom pi
```

`phantom login` opens a browser page where the user approves a short code, then saves a key on this computer. Ask the user to approve it themselves. If they already have a key, have them run `phantom login --paste` in their own terminal; never ask them to paste a key into chat.

`phantom codex`, `phantom claude` and `phantom pi` set the agent up for that run only. phantom's own flags go before the agent's arguments, with `--` between them:

```bash
phantom codex --key coding -- exec "review this repository"
```

phantom picks the key in this order: the key saved under the name in `PHANTOM_KEY_NAME`, then `PHANTOM_API_KEY`, then the key `phantom login` saved. `--key <name>` on an agent command runs it on the key saved under that name.

## Set up the user's agents for later runs

Saved setup changes the agent's own settings, so the user can start it as usual and it calls Phantom AI. Ask whether they want that or a one-run connection, unless their request already says which.

```bash
phantom setup --dry-run --table
phantom setup
phantom setup --restore
```

Show the user the dry-run changes and apply only the setup they approve. Plain `phantom setup` finds the agents on the computer and asks before it writes. Afterward the user restarts the agent or opens a new terminal. Setup keeps a copy of each file it changes, and `phantom setup --restore` puts them back.

To set up only Codex, preview that first:

```bash
phantom setup --agent codex --provider --dry-run --table
phantom setup --agent codex --provider
```

`--agent <name> --provider` writes without asking, so run it only after the user approves the preview. For Cursor, setup prints steps the user follows in Cursor's settings; pi gets the skill only. Most agents read the key through `phantom key show` or the `PHANTOM_API_KEY` line setup adds to the shell startup file. Cline is the exception: setup writes the key into Cline's own settings file, which only the user can read.

If the user asked for a budget, check that the key their agent uses has that cap. Making a second key with a cap doesn't change the key the agent already uses.

## Add credit

```bash
phantom fund --amount 10 --card
phantom fund --amount 10 --coin usdc
phantom workspace payment --id <payment-id>
```

`--card` opens Stripe Checkout in the browser. `--coin usdc` pays in USDC on Solana and `--coin usdc-base` in USDC on Base; both return a payment link and a payment id. The credit appears once Stripe confirms the payment. `phantom workspace payment --id <payment-id>` says whether it has arrived, and `phantom balance` shows the key's credit.

## Cap what keys spend

```bash
phantom keys create --save coding --limit 5
phantom keys list
phantom keys set --id coding --budget 20 --period 30 --rate 1
phantom keys revoke --id coding
phantom keys saved
phantom keys rm <name>
phantom balance
```

`--limit` caps a key's total spend, `--budget` its spend per `--period` days, and `--rate` its dollars per minute. The server enforces each cap. `--id` takes the key's name, its id, or the first 4 or more characters of its id, as `phantom keys list` shows them. Revoking a key turns it off for good; its credit stays in the workspace. `keys saved` lists the keys saved on this computer, and `keys rm` forgets one there while the key keeps working.

## Set rules for `auto`

```bash
phantom route
phantom route set --models <model-a>,<model-b>
phantom route rule add --if has_tools=true --use first
phantom route test --table
```

A route policy applies to requests for model `auto`. To change the policy of the key an agent runs with `--key coding`, set `PHANTOM_KEY_NAME=coding`. `phantom route test` costs nothing.

## Pick phantom-1, phantom-1:free or phantom-1:zdr

```bash
phantom models
phantom models use phantom-1:zdr
```

`phantom models` lists Phantom's three models, the jobs each can do and the model behind each job. `phantom-1` does every job, `phantom-1:free` is chat at $0, and `phantom-1:zdr` is chat on providers that keep none of the user's data. `models use` sets the model that `phantom claude`, `phantom codex`, `phantom pi` and the next `phantom setup` start on.

## Pick the model in each tier

```bash
phantom lineup --table
phantom lineup set --frontier <model> --standard-fallback <model>
phantom lineup reset
```

Paid phantom-1 has two tiers. It starts each task on standard and moves hard steps to frontier (a failed try, or an image). phantom-1:free runs its own free models and has no tier to pick. The lineup sets the model each tier runs, from the choices `phantom lineup` lists, and a fallback to try when that model fails. `default` in place of a model puts the tier back to its default. `lineup set` keeps the tiers you don't name.

## See what was spent

```bash
phantom spend --table
phantom spend --workspace --from 2026-09-01 --to 2026-09-30
```

`phantom spend` shows what the key spent by model and day, and an estimate of what `phantom-1` saved compared with running every call on its frontier model. `--workspace` shows every key in the workspace by name. Dates are UTC days (`YYYY-MM-DD`), and the default is this month.

## Recovery, receipts and deleting a workspace

`phantom --help --all` lists every command, including `phantom verify` for receipts, and the environment variables.

A guest workspace has no account; whoever holds its recovery file controls it. Save that file with `phantom workspace export --file <path>`, only to a private place.

`phantom workspace delete` deletes an empty workspace, with its keys and saved sign-ins. It asks first (`--yes` skips the question). The server refuses while the workspace holds credit, has a request running or has a payment in progress.

## Rules for running phantom

- Never print, log or repeat API keys, wallet secrets, management credentials or recovery files. `phantom keys show` is for shell use, not for your context.
- Change phantom's state with its commands. Don't edit or delete its files by hand.
- Ask before any payment the user hasn't asked for. Their approval covers only the payment and amount they named.
- Make lasting `phantom setup` changes only when the user asks; otherwise preview with `--dry-run`.
- If the user wants to keep using their agent's own subscription, do that. Send their agent's calls to Phantom only when they ask for it.
- Exit code 2 means the server rejected the key. Report it; don't retry with the same key.

# Phantom CLI `phantom` connects Claude Code, Codex, pi and other coding agents to [Phantom AI](https://phantom.codes), an OpenAI-compatible API. It signs you in, keeps your key on your computer, adds credit and caps what each key can spend. [Docs](https://phantom.codes/docs) · [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@phantomcodes/cli) ## Install and set up You need Node 24 or newer and the coding agent itself. ```bash npm i -g @phantomcodes/cli phantom setup ``` With no key saved yet, `phantom setup` signs you in first, with the same browser approval as `phantom login`. Then it finds the agents on your computer, shows what it will change in each file, and asks before it writes anything. Restart your agent, or open a new terminal, to use the connection. With no credit, phantom-1 runs on free models, up to 200 requests a day from a coding agent, and you don't need a card. Free calls leave out web search, which costs money on any model. If you used pai, this CLI's old name, run `phantom setup` once after you install. Until then, Claude Code and the shell block that pai wrote still call `pai`, and phantom prints a reminder. ### What setup changes Setup writes model settings for Claude Code, Codex, opencode, Continue, Goose, Aider, GitHub Copilot CLI, Cline, Gemini CLI, Crush, Qwen Code, Kilo Code, Kimi Code, Droid, Mistral Vibe and Zed. Cursor, VS Code, JetBrains AI Assistant, Warp and Trae keep these settings on their own settings screens, so setup prints the steps for you to follow. pi gets the skill only. It also installs the `phantom-ai` skill, a file that teaches the agent the phantom commands. To install the skill for one agent and change nothing else, run `phantom setup --agent claude` (or the agent's name). - `phantom setup --dry-run` shows the changes and writes nothing. - `--no-shell`, or unticking "Your shell" in the checklist, leaves your shell startup file alone. Setup then prints the lines to add yourself. - `--limit 20` caps what the key can spend each month, and `--limit none` removes the cap. At a terminal, setup asks once when the key has no cap. - `phantom setup --restore` puts back each file setup changed, from the copies it kept. A file you edited after setup keeps your edits: restore takes out only Phantom's own lines and keys, and leaves the copy beside the file. It exits 1 only when a file could not be undone. - `phantom setup --provider off` takes Phantom out of an agent and keeps the rest of its settings. In JSON settings files (Claude Code, Qwen Code, Gemini CLI and others), setup records each value it replaces and puts it back. Claude Code's background calls (titles, summaries and its Explore agent) run on the model you chose with `phantom models`, so picking `phantom-1:zdr` covers them too. ## Let your agent set it up Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or another agent that can run terminal commands: ```text Help me set up phantom for AI inference through Phantom AI. Check that I have Node 24 or newer, then install @phantomcodes/cli if needed. Run phantom setup --agent to install the phantom-ai skill, and read it. Check for an existing workspace and saved keys before changing anything. If I need to connect, start phantom login and let me complete the device approval. Check the workspace balance. Ask which coding agent I use and what budget I want, then create a named workspace key with that cap. Ask whether I want to connect my existing agent for future runs or use a temporary connection for one run. For saved setup, preview the changes with phantom setup --dry-run and show them to me before applying the setup I approve. Make sure any spending cap is on the key my agent uses. Ask before adding funds or starting paid inference. Keep keys and recovery credentials out of chat. Finish with the command to launch my agent, and explain how to undo any saved setup. ``` ## Run an agent for one session ```bash phantom login phantom fund --amount 10 --card phantom workspace status phantom codex ``` `phantom claude`, `phantom codex` and `phantom pi` start the agent with a connection that lasts for that run, and leave your saved agent settings alone. When the agent exits, phantom prints what the run spent. The agent starts on phantom-1, or on the model you picked with `phantom models`; pass `--model` after `--` to choose another. `phantom login` opens a page in your browser. You check that it shows the same short code as your terminal, approve it, and phantom saves the key on this computer (in the macOS Keychain on a Mac). If you already have a key, `phantom login --paste` saves it. Put phantom's own flags before the agent's arguments, with `--` between them: ```bash phantom codex --key coding -- exec "explain this repository" ``` ## Add credit ```bash phantom fund --amount 10 --card phantom fund --amount 10 --coin usdc ``` `--card` opens Stripe Checkout, where the total includes Stripe's card fee. `--coin usdc` pays in USDC on Solana, and `--coin usdc-base` pays in USDC on Base. The credit appears once Stripe confirms the payment. Check it with `phantom balance`. ## Give each agent its own key and cap Every key in a workspace spends from the same balance. Make one key per agent, each with its own cap: ```bash phantom keys create --save coding --limit 5 phantom claude --key coding phantom keys list phantom keys set --id coding --limit 10 ``` `phantom keys set` changes three caps: - `--limit`: the most the key can spend in total. - `--budget`: the most it can spend each month, or each `--period` days. - `--rate`: the most it can spend in one minute, in dollars. Each takes a number of zero or more, or `none`. phantom refuses a mistyped value such as `5usd` and changes nothing. `--id` takes the key's name, its id, or the first 4 or more characters of its id, as `phantom keys list` shows them. Revoking a key turns it off for good; its credit stays in the workspace. If phantom can't save a new or rotated key on this computer (a locked Keychain over SSH, for example), it prints the key once and exits with an error. Copy the key before you close the terminal. ## Choose the model Phantom has three models of its own. `phantom models` shows what each can do (chat, images in, embeddings, rerank, images, video, speech, transcription) and the model behind each job: - `phantom-1` does every job. Chat starts each task on the standard tier and moves hard steps to frontier: a failed try, or an image. - `phantom-1:free` is chat on free models at $0, with no card. - `phantom-1:zdr` is chat (with images) on providers that keep none of your data. At a terminal, `phantom models` asks which one your agents should use. To pick without the menu: ```bash phantom models use phantom-1:zdr ``` `phantom claude`, `phantom codex`, `phantom pi` and the next `phantom setup` start on the model you pick. Agents you set up earlier keep their model until you run `phantom setup` again. ### Pick the model in each tier Your key's lineup sets the model phantom-1 runs in each tier, and a fallback model to try when that one fails: ```bash phantom lineup --table phantom lineup set --frontier --standard-fallback phantom lineup reset ``` `phantom lineup` lists the models each tier can run. Write `default` in place of a model to put that tier back to its default. ### Set rules for `auto` A route policy is your key's own rules for which model answers a request for `auto`. It can prefer cheaper models, and switch models for tool use, reasoning or a budget that is running low: ```bash PHANTOM_KEY_NAME=coding phantom route set --models , PHANTOM_KEY_NAME=coding phantom route test --table ``` A request that names its own model skips the policy, unless you set `--applies-to all`. `phantom route set --sort fast` sends each request to the provider that starts answering soonest, and `--sort default` goes back to cheapest first. ## See what you spent ```bash phantom spend --table phantom spend --from 2026-09-01 --to 2026-09-30 phantom spend --workspace --table ``` Dates are UTC days, and the default is this month. Without `--workspace` you see the key you run as; with it, every key in your workspace by name. The "saved" figure compares what phantom-1 cost with the same tokens at the frontier model's price today, so it is an estimate. ## Commands by task | Task | Commands | | --- | --- | | Sign in and out | `phantom login`, `phantom logout` | | Set up your agents | `phantom setup`, `phantom setup --dry-run`, `phantom setup --restore` | | Start an agent for one run | `phantom claude`, `phantom codex`, `phantom pi` | | Add credit and check spending | `phantom fund`, `phantom balance`, `phantom spend`, `phantom workspace status` | | Manage the workspace's keys | `phantom keys create`, `phantom keys set`, `phantom keys rotate`, `phantom keys revoke` | | Manage the keys saved on this computer | `phantom keys saved`, `phantom keys save`, `phantom keys rm` | | Pick phantom-1, phantom-1:free or phantom-1:zdr | `phantom models`, `phantom models use ` | | Pick the model in each tier | `phantom lineup`, `phantom lineup set`, `phantom lineup reset` | | Set rules for `auto` | `phantom route` | | Use the providers that answer soonest | `phantom route set --sort fast` (`--sort default` for cheapest first) | ## Output and exit codes At a terminal, commands draw a screen, and choices are pickers (arrow keys, Enter, Esc to go back). When scripts and agents run them through a pipe, they print JSON on stdout and errors on stderr. `--json` prints JSON at a terminal, and `--table` draws the screen in a pipe. phantom refuses a flag it doesn't know. `phantom claude`, `phantom codex` and `phantom pi` run in your terminal and print a spending summary on stderr when the agent exits. Exit codes: 0 for success (and for Esc), 1 for an error, 2 for a rejected key, 130 for Ctrl+C. `phantom setup` returns 1 when it could only install the skills because there was no key yet (`"complete": false`). An agent run returns the agent's exit code.
Advanced and older commands `phantom --help` shows the main commands. `phantom --help --all` lists every command and flag. The older `phantom key` commands still work. `phantom keys list` reads the workspace, and `phantom keys saved` lists the keys saved on this computer. `phantom keys show` prints a saved key for shell use, as in `PHANTOM_API_KEY=$(phantom keys show)`; keep it out of chat and logs.
Development and contributing The CLI lives in `cli/` in the Phantom repo, which uses pnpm. Install once at the repo root, then run the checks from `cli/`: ```bash pnpm install cd cli pnpm typecheck pnpm test pnpm build pnpm coverage ``` Report a security problem privately to support@phantom.codes, not in a public issue.
phantom is proprietary, under the [Phantom Proprietary License](LICENSE). It lets you install and run phantom to use Phantom AI, the hosted API it calls.
